headline: Maryland Governor Discovers Billionaires Profit From Things, Demands Investigation
subheadline: Wes Moore, potential 2028 contender, shocked to learn that the people writing AI policy also benefit from AI existing.
source_headline: The people who are supposed to be helping to protect us are also the ones who are profiting.
body_html:
Maryland Governor Wes Moore appeared on "The Axios Show" this week to deliver a revelation so stunning it required cable news validation: billionaires are profiting from AI while simultaneously shaping the regulatory environment around AI. Moore, who is positioning himself as a 2028 presidential contender, expressed grave concern that Washington is leaving Americans vulnerable to unchecked artificial intelligence development because of—and we cannot overstate the boldness here—"billionaire greed and clout." This is the kind of insight that normally costs $50,000 at a Davos panel moderated by a Financial Times columnist.

The governor's theory rests on a simple observation: voters hate AI technology because they fear losing control over it. This is unquestionably true. What is less explored in Moore's framing is why voters might reasonably suspect that the people who claim to be protecting them from AI are the same people who have already cashed nine-figure checks from AI companies and venture firms betting on AI dominance. The tension Moore identified—between self-interested profit motive and public protection mandate—is not a bug in the system; it is the system's core operating principle, now playing out in real time across Silicon Valley, OpenAI's board, every major tech company's government affairs office, and yes, state governors' policy shops.

What makes Moore's observation particularly rich is that he occupies exactly the position he is criticizing. As chair of the Democratic Governors Association, Moore is not exactly insulated from the influence networks that connect state-level power brokers to venture capital and tech money. His criticism of billionaire clout shaping AI policy is correct. His implied assertion that he and his peers operate outside that influence dynamic is where the satirical gold lives. The 2028 presidential race will, inevitably, be funded by people who profit from AI policy decisions. Moore will not be an exception to this rule; he will be its most articulate spokesperson.

The core problem Moore identified—that protection and profit are aligned in ways that harm the public—is real and important. The core problem with Moore identifying it is that solutions require dismantling the very power structures from which he derives influence. Calling out billionaire greed is free messaging. Restructuring campaign finance, venture capital incentive alignment, and board composition requires actual sacrifice. Voters do fear losing control. They also sense, accurately, that the people warning them about AI risk are the same people whose net worth increases when AI risk remains unregulated.

This is not a critique of Moore personally. This is a feature of how American political economy functions. Democratic governors are as embedded in venture capital networks as Republican senators are embedded in energy company networks. The difference is merely which billionaires get to claim the moral high ground while extracting value. Moore has discovered the central hypocrisy of techno-progressive politics: you can advocate for AI safety while your largest donors profit from AI deregulation, and nobody will ask you to choose.

The real scandal would be if any politician at Moore's level actually did.
glossary_definition: A regulatory responsibility that conveniently expires whenever it conflicts with portfolio returns.
